```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3, dpi = 110)
library(viridisSYR)
library(ggplot2)
```

# What viridis optimizes, and how it is measured here

The viridis colour maps were designed by Smith and van der Walt (2015) for Matplotlib and are distributed in R
by the viridis and viridisLite packages (Garnier et al., 2024). Their design criteria are:

1. **Perceptual uniformity.** Equal steps in the data should look like equal steps in colour. This is measured
   as the colour difference between neighbouring colours in the CAM02-UCS uniform colour space (Luo et al., 2006;
   built on CIECAM02, Moroney et al., 2002). A perfectly uniform map has the same neighbour difference ΔE' at every step.
2. **Ordered lightness.** Lightness J' rises monotonically from one end to the other. This is also what makes a
   map readable in grayscale.
3. **Colourfulness.** The map should span a wide range of hue and chroma.
4. **Colour vision deficiency (CVD).** The map should stay ordered and discriminable under simulated
   deuteranomaly, protanomaly and tritanomaly (Machado et al., 2009).

`syr_metrics()` computes these for any scale, and `syr_compare()` compares scales (by default plasma and SYR).
The CAM02-UCS conversion (`cam02ucs()`) is an independent implementation of the published equations for sRGB viewing
conditions; the sanity checks are below. Everything here uses 256 colours per scale and complete (severity 1)
colour-vision-deficiency simulation.

```{r metrics}
cmp <- syr_compare()
show <- cmp[, c("scale", "deficiency", "J_start", "J_end", "J_range", "J_monotone", "J_min_step", "J_r2",
                "dE_mean", "dE_cv", "dE_max_ratio", "chroma_mean", "hue_span")]
num <- vapply(show, is.numeric, logical(1)); show[num] <- lapply(show[num], round, 3)
show
```

# Sanity checks of the CAM02-UCS implementation

Black has J' = 0 and white J' = 100, a gray ramp rises monotonically with little chroma, and viridis itself, the
map these criteria were written for, comes out as designed: lightness rises monotonically and the neighbour
differences are nearly constant.

```{r sanity}
round(cam02ucs(c("black", "white"))$Jp, 2)
m_v <- syr_metrics(viridisLite::viridis(256), "none")
c(J_monotone = m_v$J_monotone, J_r2 = round(m_v$J_r2, 4), dE_cv = round(m_v$dE_cv, 3))
```

# 1. Perceptual uniformity

```{r uniform, fig.height=3.2}
nd <- function(cols, nm) {
  u <- cam02ucs(cols); data.frame(scale = nm, position = seq(0, 1, length.out = length(cols))[-1],
                                  dE = sqrt(diff(u$Jp)^2 + diff(u$ap)^2 + diff(u$bp)^2))
}
d <- rbind(nd(viridisLite::plasma(256), "plasma"), nd(syr(256), "SYR"))
ggplot(d, aes(position, dE, colour = scale)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(plasma = "#CC4678", SYR = "#000E54")) +
  labs(x = "position on the scale", y = "ΔE' between neighbouring colours (CAM02-UCS)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r uniformtxt, echo=FALSE}
p <- cmp[cmp$scale == "plasma" & cmp$deficiency == "none", ]; s <- cmp[cmp$scale == "SYR" & cmp$deficiency == "none", ]
```

Plasma's neighbour differences have a coefficient of variation of `r round(p$dE_cv, 2)` (largest step
`r round(p$dE_max_ratio, 2)` times the mean). SYR's is `r round(s$dE_cv, 2)` (largest step `r round(s$dE_max_ratio, 2)`
times the mean). SYR is therefore less uniform than plasma, which is expected: bending the scale through two fixed
brand colours adds variation in step size. Steps are larger than plasma's across the navy-to-purple ramp (positions 0 to 0.25) and largest on the approach to the orange (about 0.5 to 0.625),
and slightly smaller just after the purple. The variation is of the same order as plasma's, but SYR does not match plasma on this criterion.

# 2. Ordered lightness and grayscale

```{r lightness, fig.height=3}
lj <- function(cols, nm) data.frame(scale = nm, position = seq(0, 1, length.out = length(cols)), Jp = cam02ucs(cols)$Jp)
d <- rbind(lj(viridisLite::plasma(256), "plasma"), lj(syr(256), "SYR"))
ggplot(d, aes(position, Jp, colour = scale)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(plasma = "#CC4678", SYR = "#000E54")) +
  labs(x = "position on the scale", y = "lightness J' (CAM02-UCS)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Both scales rise from dark to light. SYR starts darker (J' = `r round(s$J_start, 1)` against `r round(p$J_start, 1)` for plasma) and
covers a larger lightness range (`r round(s$J_range, 1)` against `r round(p$J_range, 1)`). Lightness is nearly linear in position for
both (R² = `r round(s$J_r2, 4)` for SYR and `r round(p$J_r2, 4)` for plasma). SYR is monotone within the rounding noise of 8-bit
colours (the largest dip is `r round(s$J_min_step, 3)` J', well under the 0.15 that changing one sRGB channel by 1 produces).

Grayscale conversions are shown below, from the perceptual lightness J' and from the Rec. 709 luma that most software uses:

```{r gray, fig.height=2.4}
gray_of <- function(cols, how) {
  if (how == "luma") { m <- t(grDevices::col2rgb(cols)) / 255; g <- as.vector(m %*% c(.2126, .7152, .0722)) }
  else { g <- cam02ucs(cols)$Jp / 100 }
  grDevices::gray(pmin(pmax(g, 0), 1))
}
strips <- function(pals, hows) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pals), function(nm) do.call(rbind, lapply(hows, function(h) {
    cols <- if (h == "color") pals[[nm]] else gray_of(pals[[nm]], h)
    data.frame(row = paste(nm, "-", h), x = seq(0, 1, length.out = length(cols)), col = cols)
  }))))
}
st <- strips(list(plasma = viridisLite::plasma(256), SYR = syr(256)), c("color", "J'", "luma"))
st$row <- factor(st$row, rev(unique(st$row)))
ggplot(st, aes(x, row, fill = col)) + geom_raster() + scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(x = "position on the scale", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

# 3. Colourfulness

SYR's mean chroma is `r round(s$chroma_mean, 1)` (plasma `r round(p$chroma_mean, 1)`) and its hue spans `r round(s$hue_span)`° (plasma
`r round(p$hue_span)`°). Both run blue-violet, purple, pink, orange and yellow; SYR adds a more saturated orange.

# 4. Colour vision deficiency

```{r cvd, fig.height=3.2}
cv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("none", "deutan", "protan", "tritan"), function(def) {
  f <- switch(def, none = identity, deutan = function(x) colorspace::deutan(x, 1),
              protan = function(x) colorspace::protan(x, 1), tritan = function(x) colorspace::tritan(x, 1))
  rbind(data.frame(row = paste("plasma -", def), x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 256), col = f(viridisLite::plasma(256))),
        data.frame(row = paste("SYR -", def), x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 256), col = f(syr(256))))
}))
cv$row <- factor(cv$row, rev(unique(cv$row)))
ggplot(cv, aes(x, row, fill = col)) + geom_raster() + scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(x = "position on the scale", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

```{r cvdtab}
cvd <- cmp[, c("scale", "deficiency", "J_monotone", "J_min_step", "dE_total", "dE_mean", "dE_cv")]
cvd[sapply(cvd, is.numeric)] <- lapply(cvd[sapply(cvd, is.numeric)], round, 3)
cvd
```

Under simulated CVD both scales lose some colour difference (`dE_total` falls) and become less uniform (`dE_cv` rises),
as every colour map does. Lightness stays ordered for both within the quantization tolerance, so the order of the
values remains readable. SYR's retained path length under each deficiency is
`r paste0(round(100 * cmp$dE_total[cmp$scale == "SYR" & cmp$deficiency != "none"] / s$dE_total), "%", collapse = ", ")`
of its normal-vision value for deutan, protan and tritan simulations; plasma's is
`r paste0(round(100 * cmp$dE_total[cmp$scale == "plasma" & cmp$deficiency != "none"] / p$dE_total), "%", collapse = ", ")`.

# Summary

| Criterion | plasma | SYR |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Lightness order (J′ monotone, within 8-bit noise) | yes | yes |
| Lightness range | `r round(p$J_range, 1)` | `r round(s$J_range, 1)` |
| Uniform steps (CV of neighbour ΔE′; lower is more uniform) | `r round(p$dE_cv, 2)` | `r round(s$dE_cv, 2)` |
| Mean chroma | `r round(p$chroma_mean, 1)` | `r round(s$chroma_mean, 1)` |
| Passes through Syracuse navy and orange exactly | no | yes |

viridisSYR keeps plasma's lightness order, colour sequence and grayscale behaviour and adds the two Syracuse colours,
at the cost of less uniform steps than plasma. Use plasma where perceptual uniformity is the priority, and SYR where
the Syracuse colours matter and the small loss of uniformity is acceptable.
